newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ parties in frantic 11th hour talks on coalition.
newsitem.headline: NZ parties in frantic 11th hour talks on coalition.

text.p: New Zealand political parties threw themselves into a frantic round of last minute talks on Monday on the eve of a possible announcement on a new government.
The caretaker National Party government and centre-left Labour both aim to form a coalition with nationalist New Zealand First, whose MPs were due to meet on Tuesday to make their choice.
Caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger said his party's MPs backed his coalition proposal to NZ First.
Labour leaders spent much of the day consulting the left-wing Alliance, whose support a Labour-NZ First coalition would need on confidence issues.
NZ First emerged holding the balance of power after a general election on October 12, and National and Labour have been competing throughout marathon negotiations to secure its support.
Neither will reveal what concessions it has offerd, but media reports have speculated Bolger is prepared to scrap planned tax cuts in favour of extra spending sought by NZ First.
"I think we would form a very comfortable mix, a very comfortable fit (with NZ First). Obviously there has been a lot of give and take in the negotiations," Bolger said in a radio interview.
He denied that National had placed key policies "up for grabs".
Maverick National MP John Banks, adamantly opposed to scrapping the tax cuts, said he was pleased with progress on the issue at a party meeting on Monday.

"It may mean that the tax cuts are deferred, or it may mean that we spend X amount of money in health, social welfare and education, then deliver the tax promises at a later date. I would be much more comfortable with that," he told reporters.
Labour leader Helen Clark held fresh talks with NZ First leader Winston Peters and told reporters: "We are making progress towards New Zealand First finalising its position tomorrow."
Ask how she felt personally on the eve of NZ First's decision, which could make her the country's first woman prime minister, she told reporters: "I'll sleep well."
